messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sameer, a 41-year-old graphic designer, traces the beginning of his constricted world to a single night nine months ago. He had gone to a downtown protest with a colleague who had assured him it would be a peaceful, candle-lit affair. For an hour, it was. Then came the chaos, the sudden declaration of an unlawful assembly, and the swift, violent police advance. In the confusion, he was separated from his colleague, shoved against a wall by an officer, and wrongfully arrested. The air was thick with a sharp, acrid smell he later learned was from a discharged smoke canister. What haunts him most, however, is that his colleague, who could have corroborated his story, simply watched from the crowd and later denied Sameer was even with him. The sense of that betrayal, stark and absolute, was worse than the rough hands or the zip ties.

In the weeks that followed, Sameer found he could not speak about what happened. When his wife asked, the words would not form; he knew the sequence of events, but trying to narrate them felt like assembling a puzzle with mismatched pieces. He would start, then lose the thread completely, the story dissolving into a fog of shame. He felt an intense, burning guilt whenever he tried to recall the details, a feeling that he must have done something to deserve it, to be abandoned so completely. This fragmented, guilt-laden memory became the anchor for his new way of being. He began avoiding any situation that required planning for the future, a deep-seated dread making it impossible to book a flight or even commit to dinner plans for the following week, as if he no longer had the right to expect good things to happen.

His design work, once a source of joy, became a minefield. His belief that the world was a dangerous place, a place where anyone could turn on you without warning, made him acutely sensitive to any sign of authority. He began to see threats everywhere, and the sight of a security guard in a client’s lobby or even a mail carrier in uniform was enough to send a jolt of panic through him. These encounters would instantly reactivate the memory, not as a coherent story, but as a bodily sensation of dread and the scent of burning chemicals in his nostrils. His conviction that he had been betrayed by someone he trusted made him constantly replay the memory, searching for the moment he should have known better, a mental flagellation that only deepened the guilt.

This constant state of alert has reshaped his behaviour into a series of rigid, self-protective rituals. Before any interaction, whether a client call or a trip to the grocery store, Sameer now rehearses precisely what he will say, scripting his words to avoid any possible misstep that could draw negative attention. He is relentlessly hypervigilant, his eyes constantly scanning crowds for anyone who looks official or out of place. This constant scanning, of course, makes him far more likely to spot the very uniforms that trigger him, creating a feedback loop of anxiety. The hypervigilance also serves as daily confirmation of his core belief: the world is indeed a dangerous place that requires his constant watchfulness. By keeping himself in this state of high alert and mentally rehearsing perceived threats, he never allows the traumatic memory to be filed away as something that is over. It remains immediate, a present danger he must manage moment to moment.

The cycle has tightened its grip over the last few months. His avoidance of future plans has put a significant strain on his marriage. His wife, frustrated and hurt by his inability to commit to a simple vacation, finally gave him an ultimatum. The thought of losing her was the one thing that broke through the paralysis. Sameer now sits in therapy, his world shrunk to his apartment and the few client sites he cannot avoid. He can’t find the words to explain the night of the protest clearly, but he can articulate the fear that governs him now: a certainty that people cannot be trusted, and that safety is an illusion. He hopes, more than anything, to one day feel secure enough to believe in a future again.
